lede: Four words change the whole question: given that. They tell you something has already happened, so the group you are choosing from is smaller than it was. Everything about conditional probability is deciding which smaller group goes on the bottom of the fraction.
can: Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree
Use the formula on the sheet, with the condition on the denominator
Spot when one event sits inside another, so the numerator is the smaller one

md:
A cafe asks 250 customers whether they drink tea or coffee and which age group they are in.
Ask 'what is the probability a customer drinks tea' and the group is all 250. Add 'given that the customer is under 30' and the group is only the under-30s. Nothing else about the table has changed.

prompt: On the cafe table, how many of the 250 customers are under 30?
explain: $42 + 108 = 150$: the under-30 column's two cells. That total is the group any 'given under 30' question divides by.

md:
'The probability of tea, given under 30' is written $P(\text{tea} \mid \text{under 30})$. The upright bar is read 'given'.
The condition, under 30, is the group you are now choosing from. So the 42 under-30 tea drinkers go over the 150 under-30s: $\dfrac{42}{150} = \dfrac{7}{25}$, which is $0.28$.

prompt: On the cafe table, which total is the denominator of $P(\text{tea} \mid \text{under 30})$?
explain: The condition names the under-30s, so those 150 are the group you are choosing from. Dividing by 250 would ignore the condition altogether.

md:
Divide the top and the bottom of $\dfrac{42}{150}$ by the 250 asked. The fraction does not change, but its two parts become probabilities:
$\dfrac{42}{150} = \dfrac{42/250}{150/250}$
The top is now $P(\text{tea and under 30})$ and the bottom $P(\text{under 30})$.

That is the formula printed on page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet: $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. A table question can be answered straight from the counts; a tree question, where only probabilities are given, uses the formula as printed.

prompt: In $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, which probability goes on the bottom?
explain: The condition is the new whole group, so it is the denominator. The numerator is the probability that both happen.

text: Why a share can come out bigger

title: Why dividing works
md: Conditioning is rescaling. The condition's probability is the new whole, so dividing by it turns the joint probability into a share of the smaller group. That is also why a conditional probability can be larger than the joint one it came from.

In the cafe table $P(\text{tea and under 30})$ is $0.168$ and $P(\text{under 30})$ is $0.6$. Rescaling: $0.168 \div 0.6 = 0.28$, bigger than the joint probability, because the group is smaller than the whole survey.

explain: Rescale by the condition: $0.21 \div 0.28 = 0.75$. The share of the smaller group is larger than the joint probability, as it always is when $P(B)$ is below 1.

text: 3. The same table, the other way round

md:
$P(\text{under 30} \mid \text{tea})$ is a different question. The condition is now 'drinks tea', so the group is the 75 in that row, and the same 42 go on top.
Same cell on top, different total underneath, different answer.

The coffee row shows it with other numbers:
$P(\text{coffee} \mid \text{under 30}) = \dfrac{108}{150}$
$P(\text{under 30} \mid \text{coffee}) = \dfrac{108}{175}$
Read the condition before anything else.

explain: $\dfrac{42}{75}$ is $\dfrac{14}{25}$. The condition is the tea row this time, so 75 is the denominator.

text: 4. See it done: a Venn diagram

md:
110 students take French, Spanish, both or neither. 70 take French, 45 take Spanish, 24 take both.
**Step 1.** Fill the regions: French only 46, both 24, Spanish only 21, neither 19. They total 110.
**Step 2.** Read the condition. 'Given that the student takes French' means the group is the 70 in that circle.
**Step 3.** $P(\text{Spanish} \mid \text{French}) = \dfrac{24}{70}$, which is $\dfrac{12}{35}$.

text: 5. From a tree: add the branches

md:
A match is cancelled more often after rain. $P(\text{rain}) = 0.3$; the match is cancelled with probability $0.5$ after rain and $0.1$ on a dry day.
There are no counts, so each path is a product: rain and cancelled is $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$, and dry and cancelled is $0.7 \times 0.1 = 0.07$.

prompt: On the match tree, the rain-and-cancelled branch is $0.15$ and the dry-and-cancelled branch is $0.07$. What is $P(\text{cancelled})$?
explain: $0.15 + 0.07 = 0.22$. Two separate branches both end in 'cancelled', so they add.

md:
$P(\text{rain} \mid \text{cancelled})$ is $P(\text{rain and cancelled})$ divided by $P(\text{cancelled})$: one branch over the sum of both cancelled branches.
The numerator is one branch; the denominator is every branch that satisfies the condition. Finding one of the two and stopping is the commonest way this part is lost.
The dry days show the division done: given that the match was cancelled, the day was dry with probability $0.07 \div 0.22 = \dfrac{7}{22}$, about $0.32$.

title: Conditional Probability
why: Conditional probability from tables and from trees, in the notation this unit uses. The reversed-condition trap and the nested-event case are the steps this unit adds on top.

title: What the reports keep finding
md: Candidates often reach the right numerator, or the right denominator, but never combine the two. Write the formula with the condition named before any number goes in.

prompt: Using the match tree, $P(\text{rain and cancelled}) = 0.15$ and $P(\text{cancelled}) = 0.22$. What is $P(\text{rain} \mid \text{cancelled})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: $\dfrac{0.15}{0.22}$ is $\dfrac{15}{22}$, which is 0.682. Giving 0.15 on its own leaves the division undone.

text: 7. When one event sits inside the other

md:
Four coins are tossed. Ask for $P(\text{four heads} \mid \text{at least two heads})$.
Four heads **is** at least two heads, so the two events together are just the smaller one: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)$. There is nothing to multiply on the numerator.
So the top is $P(\text{four heads}) = \dfrac{1}{16}$ and the bottom $P(\text{at least two}) = \dfrac{11}{16}$, giving $\dfrac{1}{16} \div \dfrac{11}{16} = \dfrac{1}{11}$.

explain: Every outcome with four heads already has at least two, so the two events together are the inner event on its own. Multiplying would treat them as unrelated.

text: 8. Expected numbers from a conditional probability

md:
A conditional probability scales a group, and the group it scales is the one named in the condition.
If the cafe expects 500 customers under 30 next week, the expected number drinking tea is $500 \times \dfrac{7}{25} = 140$.
The whole survey's share would give $500 \times \dfrac{42}{250} = 84$, far too few.

caption: Next week's customers are all under 30, so the ringed column is the one that scales them.

prompt: In the cafe survey, 108 of the 150 customers under 30 drink coffee. The cafe expects 500 customers under 30 next week. How many of them would you expect to drink coffee?
explain: $500 \times \dfrac{108}{150} = 360$. The 500 is the group the condition names, so that is what gets scaled, and with the 140 tea drinkers it makes the 500.

md: **No 'given' in the words.** Summer 2023 stated the condition as a sentence of its own, and many answers came over the whole group. 'A customer picked from those aged 30 and over' is a condition too: of those 100, 33 drink tea, $\dfrac{33}{100} = 0.33$.

**The condition is the second stage.** Summer 2025 gave the result of a second set and asked about the first. Two beads come from 6 red and 4 green; given the second is red, the first was red with probability $\dfrac{30}{30 + 24} = \dfrac{5}{9}$, counted out of 90.

prompt: Two beads are taken without replacement from 6 red and 4 green. Given that the second bead is green, what is the probability that the first was red? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: Out of 90, red then green is 24 and green then green is 12. Given the second is green: $\dfrac{24}{24 + 12}$, which is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

md: **The condition is a 'not'.** Summer 2025 also conditioned on a student who does not study a subject. Given the match was not cancelled, the whole is $P(\text{played}) = 1 - 0.22 = 0.78$, the two 'played' branches together.

**The overlap is not given.** With $P(A) = 0.7$, $P(B) = 0.36$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, the addition rule finds it first: $0.7 + 0.36 - 0.8 = 0.26$. Then $P(A \mid B)$ is $0.26 \div 0.36 = \dfrac{13}{18}$.

explain: The overlap first: $0.6 + 0.45 - 0.75 = 0.3$. The condition is $A$, so $0.3 \div 0.6 = 0.5$.

text: Going further: 'at least one' as the condition

md:
The hardest shape on the paper: Summer 2026 ended its tree question with a condition of 'during the weekend', that is, on at least one day. Snow falls on each day of a weekend with probability $0.1$, the days independent.
The whole is $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.19$.

Given snow on at least one day, no snow on Sunday means snow on Saturday only: $0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09$, and $0.09 \div 0.19 = \dfrac{9}{19}$. The top sits inside the condition, so nothing more is multiplied.

prompt: On the same snowy weekend, given that it snows on at least one of the two days, what is the probability that it snows on both? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: Both days is $0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01$, and it sits inside 'at least one', so $0.01 \div 0.19 = \dfrac{1}{19}$.

md:
Read the condition first and write down the group it names.
Use $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, with the condition underneath.
Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree, in either direction.
Use the inner event as the numerator when one event sits inside another.
Scale the group the condition names when an expected number is asked for.

This is the last part of a probability question, and the one that separates the strongest. It is worded 'given that', or 'a person is chosen from those who', for two or three marks. The first mark is the right denominator; the last is the divided answer. Stuck: write the formula with the condition named, then fill in the two pieces.
